Several open-source CLIs match this description. I didn't check licenses, maintenance status, or current versions, so verify those before adopting one.

- **leakguard** (Rust, zero-dependency) looks like the closest fit. It redacts secrets & PII from stdin (or files) and writes to stdout. Its examples include piping `tail -f` into it, and it covers emails, credit cards, IPs, JWTs, API keys, and more. A `--check` mode exits non-zero when sensitive data is found, and the --mask option offers label, fixed, char, partial, and hash modes.
- **hexredact** focuses on reversible redaction for logs. Its stdout carries only the redacted text, since UI output goes to stderr. It gives the same value the same token, so you can still follow one IP or user through the logs. It also handles IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, tagging them as public, private, or reserved.
- **cleansh** (Rust) is designed to sanitize terminal output for safe sharing. It covers common email formats and both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. It takes piped input or files, with flexible options for custom rules and output formats.
- **local-redact** (Python) finds email addresses, phone numbers, IBANs, card numbers, IP addresses and API keys. It also supports a JSON report and a --check flag that exits 1 if anything was found.
- **rog7/redact** (Python) is a simpler option: it hides emails, API keys, and tokens in a log before you share it. The cleaned log is printed to stdout, and the original file is not changed.

For a pipeline that needs stdin-to-stdout filtering with an IP and email focus, leakguard and cleansh look like the best starting points. hexredact fits if you need consistent tokens across a log. The rest are narrower or more specialized.

content.content:
**leakguard 1.0.0** (released 2026-10-06)

- **Description:** A zero-dependency Rust library and CLI for redacting secrets and PII from text and logs.
- **License:** Dual-licensed under MIT or Apache-2.0, at your option.
- **Repository:** https://github.com/ptukovar/leakguard
- **Install:**
  - CLI: `cargo install leakguard`
  - Library: add `leakguard = "1.0.0"` to `[dependencies]`

**Stdin-to-stdout usage**

```
tail -f app.log | leakguard
leakguard --only email,ipv4 --mask char --char '#' < input.txt
```

**Detected patterns (default)**

- Email, credit card (Luhn-checked), IPv4, IPv6, JWT
- US SSN, MAC address, IBAN (mod-97 checked)
- AWS access keys, Google API keys, Stripe keys, OpenAI keys
- GitHub, Slack, Telegram, and Discord tokens
- URL credentials, Azure connection strings, PEM private keys

**Opt-in patterns**

- `PhoneNumber`
- `GenericSecret` (high-entropy, via `HighEntropy`)

**CLI flags**

- **Masking:** `--mask` (partial, template, char), `--keep`, `--template`, `--char`
- **Selection:** `--only`, `--without`
- **Allowlist and custom words:** `--ignore`, `--redact-word`, `--redact-literal`
- **Output:** `--stats`, `--json`, `--show-values`, `--list-kinds`
- **CI checks:** `--check`, `--verbose`

Exit codes: 0 for success (including no findings under `--check`), 1 when `--check` finds a match, and 2 for a usage or I/O error.

- **License:** MIT OR Apache-2.0 for the CLI and core library. The page says the PolyForm license was retired for v0.1.9 and later. SaaS features such as `cleansh profiles sync` are inactive stubs in the open-source CLI.
- **Repository:** https://github.com/KarmaYama/cleansh-workspace
- **Install:** `cargo install cleansh`. Prebuilt binaries are available from GitHub Releases, and the page also gives source build steps (`cargo build --release`).
- **Usage (stdin):** Pipe input into the tool, for example `echo "My email is test@example.com" | cleansh sanitize`. The page doesn't explicitly state the output destination, but the examples imply stdout. Other flags include `-c` (copy to clipboard) and `-d` (diff view).
- **Detected patterns:**
  - Emails
  - IPv4 and IPv6 addresses
  - JWTs
  - GitHub PATs
  - Stripe keys
  - AWS, GCP, and Azure cloud keys
  - SSH keys and generic hex/tokens
  - Credit cards, US SSNs, UK NINOs, and South African IDs
  - Paths, such as `/home/user` becoming `~/`
  - An opt-in Entropy Engine (`--engine entropy`) that flags high-randomness tokens without a known format
- **Latest version:** 0.1.11, released 2025-12-20.
- **Network/telemetry:** The page doesn't say whether the tool makes network calls or collects telemetry. Its dependency list includes `reqwest`, but the page doesn't explain what it's used for.

content.text:
**My pick: [leakguard](https://github.com/ptukovar/leakguard).** It's a small Rust command-line tool, dual-licensed MIT/Apache-2.0, with no dependencies. It reads from stdin, writes the redacted text to stdout, and runs entirely on your machine. The patterns are already built in, so you don't write any regexes.

**What it catches by default:** emails, IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, JWTs, AWS, Google, Stripe and OpenAI keys, GitHub, Slack, Telegram and Discord tokens, passwords inside URLs, Azure connection strings, PEM private keys, plus credit cards, SSNs, MAC addresses and IBANs. It can also flag any random-looking string as a possible secret (the generic "high-entropy" detector), but that's off by default and you have to turn it on.

## Install

I'm assuming you have the Rust toolchain or are willing to install it. The tool is installed through Cargo, Rust's package manager.

```bash
# Only if you don't already have cargo (Rust's official installer):
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh
source "$HOME/.cargo/env"

cargo install leakguard
leakguard --list-kinds    # shows the exact names of the things it can detect
```

## First run

```bash
# 1. Test on a sample first and compare the output with the original
leakguard --stats < server.log > server.redacted.log
diff <(head -200 server.log) <(head -200 server.redacted.log) | less

# 2. Normal use: pipe a log through it
journalctl -u myapp --since "1 hour ago" | leakguard > for-ai.txt
tail -n 500 /var/log/nginx/error.log | leakguard

# 3. Also scrub your own internal hostnames or names it can't know about
cat app.log | leakguard --redact-word mycorp.internal --redact-word db-prod-01
```

Use `--only` and `--without` to choose which patterns run, and `--mask` to change how redacted values look. To turn on the random-string detector, find its exact name in `--list-kinds` and add it with `--only`. If you do that, list the default kinds you still want as well. I haven't checked whether `--only` replaces the default set or adds to it, so look at the output to be sure. `--check` exits with code 1 if it finds anything, which is handy in scripts.

## Caveats

- **It's young.** Version 1.0.0 came out on 2026-10-06 and looks like a one-person project. Read through the source before you trust it, and pin the version.
- **Pattern matching has gaps.** It will miss secrets in formats it doesn't know: custom session IDs, internal hostnames, usernames, and keys inside unusual config formats. Always skim the output before you paste it. `--redact-word` handles known internal strings.
- **IPs:** it redacts all of them, including harmless ones like `127.0.0.1`. If you want to keep some, `--ignore` lets you allowlist values.

## Alternatives

- **[cleansh](https://docs.rs/crate/cleansh/latest)** (Rust, MIT/Apache-2.0): `cargo install cleansh`, then `cat app.log | cleansh sanitize`. It covers similar ground, also shortens home paths to `~/`, and has an opt-in random-string detector (`--engine entropy`). It pulls in an HTTP library and has inactive paid-service stubs. If you need a guarantee that nothing leaves the machine, check the source or run it with no network access.
- **[hexredact](https://github.com/happygream/hexredact):** replaces each value with a token, and the same value always gets the same token. That lets the AI still follow, say, "IP_3" through the whole log, and you can reverse it afterwards.
- **[rog7/redact](https://github.com/rog7/redact)** and **[local-redact](https://github.com/sumankrsh/local-redact)** (Python): simpler, smaller pattern sets.
- Gitleaks and TruffleHog are better known, but they report secrets rather than filtering text through, so they don't fit stdin-to-stdout use.

I didn't install or run any of these. The details above come from their docs.rs and GitHub pages.

- [leakguard on docs.rs](https://docs.rs/crate/leakguard/latest) / [source](https://docs.rs/crate/leakguard/latest/source/src/bin/leakguard.rs)
- [cleansh on docs.rs](https://docs.rs/crate/cleansh/latest) / [cleansh crate docs](https://docs.rs/cleansh/0.1.7/i686-unknown-linux-gnu/cleansh/)
- [hexredact](https://github.com/happygream/hexredact)
- [rog7/redact](https://github.com/rog7/redact)
- [local-redact](https://github.com/sumankrsh/local-redact)
